/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The kitchen serves a hot lunch at noon and packs extra meals for people who cannot stay, so the work is not only cooking; we also check names, sort containers, and make sure the drivers get the right number of bags. I arrived at 6:40 with my blue apron and the clipboard from the office and found the side entrance open, but the main room lights were still off. I thought the gas burner had not been checked, but Rosa showed me the green mark on the board and said it had already been checked at six. The freezer reading was minus eighteen and the refrigerator was four degrees, so we logged both before moving the milk.

Marta was coordinating the shift, and she had taped a paper schedule beside the handwashing sink. She said the bread van would come Tuesday—no, Thursday—at about 8:15, and I repeated Thursday on the delivery sheet because the first day was a slip. She asked me to check the count on the dry goods shelf before the drivers arrived. There were twenty-four cans of tomatoes, nine bags of lentils, and three cartons of rice. The rice carton on the bottom had a split corner, but the inner bag was intact, so we moved it to a clean bin and marked the outer carton for disposal. The flour was still sealed and dated for next month, which meant it could be used today. I said, “Right,” when Marta asked if that count made sense, and she nodded because the totals matched her list.

At seven, the first volunteer arrived carrying a folded table and two boxes of paper cups. He was new, so I showed him where to leave his coat and how to use the handwashing station before touching produce. Then Rosa washed the carrots while I rinsed celery and cut the bruised ends into the compost tub. We had thirty-six carrots and eleven celery stalks for the soup, and Marta asked us to save the leafy carrot tops for stock rather than throw them away. The soup recipe was on an index card and called for cumin, bay leaves, onions, lentils, and vegetable stock. There was a question about salt because the stock already contained some, so we left the salt tin closed until the soup was nearly finished and could be tasted.

1. Check the temperatures and write them on the sheet.
2. Count the bread and meal containers when they arrive.
3. Keep the allergy labels with the trays.
4. Tell Marta if a driver is more than ten minutes late.

Those were the four reminders I added to the shift clipboard after Rosa said people often remembered the cooking and forgot the handoff notes. A volunteer called Joao read the list and said, “Beleza”—that means okay or great in the way he was using it—and then asked if he could take the container count at the loading table. I said yes, but asked him to wait for the labels before stacking anything because the lunch trays had two different dietary groups.

Just before eight, the bread van was not there, and Marta checked her phone. She had a message from the bakery saying the driver was delayed by a flat tire and would arrive closer to nine. The condition on the meal plan was important: if the bread arrived after nine, we would pack the soup and fruit first and leave the bread bags open until the delivery came, so the crusts would not get crushed under the hot containers. Marta said she would call the community center if we had to change the pickup time, but she did not make that call yet. Rosa turned the soup down to a low simmer, and I wrote the delay on the whiteboard with the time of the message.

While we waited, Joao arranged the clean containers into stacks of ten and checked each lid for a crack. He found two that did not close and put them in the recycling tub instead of with the meal supplies. The produce box also held six apples with soft spots, and we cut those areas away for the staff snack rather than send them with the lunches because the fruit portions had to be firm enough to travel. Marta checked the allergen folder and reminded us that one tray needed a label saying “contains dairy.” The rest of the soup was dairy free, but the bread could not be assumed safe because the bakery used shared equipment. We kept that note beside the bread count instead of making a promise we could not verify.

At 8:50, the van arrived, and the driver carried in four baskets of rolls and a paper slip with the order total. Thirty-eight rolls were plain and twelve were seeded. Marta counted them while Joao marked the numbers on the clipboard. We had expected forty plain rolls, so she called the bakery and asked whether two were still in the van. The driver checked and said the missing rolls had been left at the shop by mistake. He offered to bring them later, but Marta said we needed to know the time before changing the packing plan. He called the shop and came back with an estimate of twenty minutes, so we sealed the fruit cups and packed soup while keeping the bread bags open.

At 9:15, the two plain rolls arrived in a small paper sack, and Marta checked that the count was now forty plain and twelve seeded. The lunch pickup stayed at 11:45, and she did not need to call the community center. The kitchen served soup with separate rolls, and Joao put the dairy warning card next to the seeded bread basket as instructed. The drivers signed for twenty-seven standard meals and eleven dairy free meals, and each bag had a fruit cup, a spoon, and a folded napkin. One person asked whether we could add another soup container for a neighbor who had missed the sign-up. We had two spare portions, and Marta approved one after checking the count for the later route. The other spare stayed in the refrigerator with a date label.

Before I left, I wiped the loading table, returned the clipboard to the office hook, and checked that the back door latched after the last driver went out. Rosa said the soup had been a little thicker than usual because the lentils absorbed more liquid while the van was delayed, so she wrote that note on the recipe card for the next shift. The freezer and refrigerator readings were still within the marked range when we checked them again, and Marta signed the sheet. I left the clean bin beside the dry goods shelf so the next team could see where the damaged rice carton had been moved. The final note on the board said to confirm the bakery count before starting the lunch labels and to keep the dairy warning beside the seeded rolls until the baskets were empty."}]
